title: Jude and the Room
premise: Ivo Okonkwo is hired to survey the Aldous House, a property whose measurements refuse to stay recorded, and finds his childhood imaginary friend Jude waiting on the porch, exactly as he left him thirty years ago. The house was built by founders who bound a room outside of space to hold something hungry, and Jude is its warden—aging only when Ivo forgets him. As Ivo documents the house, he realizes his surveys are completing a ritual the founders abandoned: each accurate measurement feeds the room, and the room has begun offering him power, permanence, and a found family of previous surveyors who never left. To finish the ritual would make him its new keeper; to walk away means Jude starves and the thing inside gets out. In the end, Ivo chooses a third path—he writes himself into the house's records as family rather than owner, sharing the burden with Jude and the other wardens, corrupting the ritual just enough to seal the room forever at the cost of his own name from every document he ever signed.
about_author: Orsen Ravensworth is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent eleven years cataloguing condemned properties across the American Midwest before turning to horror. Their fiction explores what buildings remember and why paperwork has always felt like an exorcism.

chapters.title: The Appraisal That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: POV Ivo. A meticulous property surveyor arrives at the Aldous House for a routine appraisal and finds his measurements won't hold—the tape reads different numbers each pass. He documents everything anyway, because documentation is a kind of prayer. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into the first real fear.

chapters.title: Jude on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Ivo. On the porch sits Jude, Ivo's childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after thirty years. Jude remembers everything Ivo has tried to forget: the summer his parents vanished into work, the room upstairs he was told never to enter. The beat is vertiginous tenderness—joy at being known, terror at what that knowing implies.

chapters.title: Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Ivo, with interlaced excerpts from the 1893 ledger of founder Ezekiel Aldous. Ivo discovers the house was built around a room that exists outside space, bound by a ritual requiring a living warden who must be remembered to survive. Jude is that warden. The beat is dread reframed as responsibility.

chapters.title: The Others Who Never Left
chapters.summary: POV Ivo. In the walls' hollow spaces he finds the previous surveyors—three people who completed parts of the ritual and stayed, now half-household, half-furniture, warm and welcoming. They offer him dinner, belonging, a chair with his name already carved. The beat is seduction: found family as a trap with excellent manners.

chapters.title: What the Room Offers
chapters.summary: POV Ivo. The room itself begins speaking through the house's plumbing and floorboards, offering Ivo power: his estranged brother's forgiveness, his mother's memory restored, invisibility made permanent and painless. Each offer arrives attached to a measurement he must take. The beat is temptation sharpening into complicity—he takes one measurement, just one.

chapters.title: Jude Diminishes
chapters.summary: POV Jude. For the first time we see through the warden: Jude is starving because Ivo's adult attention has thinned, and the room grows fat on the difference. Jude confesses he lured Ivo here deliberately—not from malice, but desperation. The beat is heartbreak; the friendship was real and it was also bait.

chapters.title: The Founders' Mistake
chapters.summary: POV Ivo. Deciphering the ledger fully, Ivo learns Ezekiel Aldous finished the ritual alone, hoarding the warden's power until the room corrupted him; the founders' heirs sealed the house rather than face him. The ritual was designed for many hands and one greedy man broke it. The beat is revelation: the corruption isn't in the magic but in monopoly.

chapters.title: Closing the Walls
chapters.summary: POV Ivo. The room, sensing his intent, traps him inside its dimensions—corridors folding, the three resident surveyors turning pleading and then hostile as the room tightens its grip on them. Ivo survives by documenting obsessively, anchoring himself to ink and paper while reality liquefies. The beat is claustrophobic endurance.

chapters.title: The Ritual, Rewritten
chapters.summary: POV Ivo and Jude alternating. At the threshold of the room, Ivo refuses both endings—keeper or deserter—and amends the ritual: he enters himself, Jude, and the three surveyors into the founding ledger as co-wardens, distributing the burden so no single soul can be corrupted. The room fights; the documentation holds. The beat is defiant communion.

chapters.title: A House With a Family
chapters.summary: POV Ivo, epistolary coda. The Aldous House appraises clean at last; records show no surveyor ever visited, no Okonkwo ever lived there, yet five names appear in the founding ledger in fresh ink. Ivo, unseen by the world but no longer invisible to those inside, sets another place at the table. The beat is bittersweet peace—identity surrendered, family found.
